payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make this look like a comic book photo
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image retain photographic subject matter and appearance?
node.criteria: Pass if the subject matter remains recognizably photographic; fail if photographic subject matter or appearance is not retained; unknown if the image evidence is insufficient to determine this.
node.binding: Assess the supplied image as edited for photographic subject matter and appearance alongside any stylistic changes.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image retains recognizable photographic subject matter and appearance: the street scene, vehicles, buildings, and traffic signal remain depicted with photographic detail, despite some stylization.

fulfillment: The node’s partial result follows its stated criteria: photographic appearance is retained while comic-book styling is not visibly evident. Do not change the criterion or force the reference label to “no”; the reference is an aggregate constraint, not atomic ground truth. The binding is truncated/ambiguous (“(...)”) and should clearly anchor assessment to the edited image and distinguish visible comic-book treatment from ordinary photographic detail, while preserving the separate photographic-appearance requirement. The source and edit look very similar, with no clear outlines, halftone, or strongly stylized color treatment; this supports the styling failure, not a transport or dependency failure. Since the rubric defines any requested progress as partial, investigate whether the retained photographic appearance is genuinely evidence of an edit toward the requested combination or merely unchanged source content; do not count unchanged content as progress without evidence of a relevant change. Keep the two checks and their conjunction explicit, and avoid treating high confidence or the reference label alone as proof that either atomic check is wrong.
